claim: The initially homogeneous epithelium of the early Drosophila embryo differentiates into regional subpopulations with different behaviours and physical properties that are needed for morphogenesis.
source: The initially homogeneous epithelium of the early Drosophila embryo differentiates into regional subpopulations with different behaviours and physical properties that are needed for morphogenesis.
evidence: This is a statement about the developmental biology of Drosophila embryos, drawing from established scientific knowledge about embryonic development.

claim: The factors at top of the genetic hierarchy that control these behaviours are known, but many of their targets are not.
source: The factors at top of the genetic hierarchy that control these behaviours are known, but many of their targets are not.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field and identifies a gap in understanding.

claim: 6111 protein groups were detected in the study.
source: We detected 6111 protein groups and 6259 phosphosites of which 3398 and 3433 were differentially regulated, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 6259 phosphosites were detected in the study.
source: We detected 6111 protein groups and 6259 phosphosites of which 3398 and 3433 were differentially regulated, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 3398 protein groups were differentially regulated.
source: We detected 6111 protein groups and 6259 phosphosites of which 3398 and 3433 were differentially regulated, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 3433 phosphosites were differentially regulated.
source: We detected 6111 protein groups and 6259 phosphosites of which 3398 and 3433 were differentially regulated, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The changes in phosphosite abundance did not correlate with changes in host protein abundance.
source: The changes in phosphosite abundance did not correlate with changes in host protein abundance, showing phosphorylation to be a regulatory step during gastrulation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of proteomic and phosphoproteomic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Phosphorylation is a regulatory step during gastrulation.
source: The changes in phosphosite abundance did not correlate with changes in host protein abundance, showing phosphorylation to be a regulatory step during gastrulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that phosphosite changes are independent of protein abundance changes.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of protein groups identified clusters that contain known fate determinants such as Doc1, Sog, Snail, and Twist.
source: Hierarchical clustering of protein groups and phosphosites identified clusters that contain known fate determinants such as Doc1, Sog, Snail, and Twist.
evidence: This is based on the clustering analysis performed on the proteomic data.

claim: The recovery of the appropriate known marker proteins in each of the different mutants validated the approach.
source: The recovery of the appropriate known marker proteins in each of the different mutants we used validated the approach, but also revealed that two mutations that both interfere with the dorsal fate pathway, Toll10B and serpin27aex do this in very different manners.
evidence: This is an inference based on the detection of expected marker proteins in the experimental data.

claim: Toll10B and serpin27aex mutations interfere with the dorsal fate pathway in very different manners.
source: The recovery of the appropriate known marker proteins in each of the different mutants we used validated the approach, but also revealed that two mutations that both interfere with the dorsal fate pathway, Toll10B and serpin27aex do this in very different manners.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the proteomic profiles of the two mutants.

claim: Diffused network analyses within each cluster point to microtubule components as one of the main groups of regulated proteins.
source: Diffused network analyses within each cluster point to microtubule components as one of the main groups of regulated proteins.
evidence: This is based on the network analysis performed on the clustered proteomic data.

claim: Microtubules have different functions in different domains along the DV axis of the embryo.
source: Functional studies on the role of microtubules provide the proof of principle that microtubules have different functions in different domains along the DV axis of the embryo.
evidence: This is based on functional perturbation experiments with colcemid presented in the manuscript.

claim: Drosophila gastrulation is initiated by the formation of a ventral furrow that leads to the internalization of the mesoderm.
source: Drosophila gastrulation is probably one of the best studied embryo-scale morphogenetic processes: it is initiated by the formation of a ventral furrow that leads to the internalization of the mesoderm.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila development.

claim: The internalization of the mesoderm causes the ventral displacement of the neuroectoderm.
source: The internalization of the mesoderm causes the ventral displacement of the neuroectoderm, the ectodermal cell population on the lateral side of the embryo, in the absence of particular cell shape behaviors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila gastrulation, supported by the cited reference (Leptin and Grunewald, 1990; Rauzi et al., 2015).

claim: The ventral displacement of the neuroectoderm is accommodated by the stretching of dorsal ectodermal cells.
source: Finally, this ventral displacement of the neuroectoderm is accommodated by the stretching of dorsal ectodermal cells (Leptin and Grunewald, 1990; Rauzi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila gastrulation, supported by the cited references.

claim: Most of the cellular components pre-exist in the egg, having been provided maternally during oogenesis either as RNA or as protein.
source: Most of the cellular components pre-exist in the egg, having been provided maternally during oogenesis either as RNA or as protein.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila embryonic development.

claim: With the exception of the determinants for anterior-posterior (AP) and dorso-ventral (DV) patterning most of these proteins are distributed throughout the early embryo.
source: With the exception of the determinants for anterior-posterior (AP) and dorso-ventral (DV) patterning most of these proteins are distributed throughout the early embryo.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila embryonic development, supported by the cited reference (Gilmour et al., 2017).

claim: Adherens junctions and the acto-myosin meshwork are dramatically remodeled in ventral cells.
source: For example, adherens junctions and the acto-myosin meshwork are dramatically remodeled in ventral cells (Rauzi et al., 2015; Kölsch et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: A gradient of the transcription factor Dorsal with its high point in nuclei on the ventral side is triggered by a graded extracellular signal that is transmitted through the transmembrane receptor Toll.
source: Briefly, a gradient of the transcription factor Dorsal with its high point in nuclei on the ventral side is triggered by a graded extracellular signal that is transmitted through the transmembrane receptor Toll (Moussian and Roth, 2005; Roth et al., 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila DV patterning, supported by the cited references.

claim: Female flies that are homozygous for certain alleles of Toll, serpin27A and gastrulation defective mutations lay eggs that develop into embryos in which all cells express genes characteristic for only one domain of the normal embryo.
source: Female flies that are homozygous for certain alleles of these mutations, or combinations of alleles, lay eggs that develop into embryos in which all cells express genes characteristic for only one domain of the normal embryo – either the ventral domain or the lateral or the dorsal domain – and to which we refer here as ventralized, lateralized, or dorsalized.
evidence: This is established knowledge about these Drosophila mutants.

claim: Phosphorylation is fast and reversible and plays key roles during early embryogenesis.
source: Among protein-level post-translational modifications, phosphorylation is fast and reversible and plays key roles during early embryogenesis: from regulating elements in the Toll and Dpp pathways, to the activation of the Rho Pathway within the mesoderm (Moussian and Roth, 2005; Martin, 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge about phosphorylation in development, supported by the cited references.

claim: Phosphorylation regulates elements in the Toll and Dpp pathways and activates the Rho Pathway within the mesoderm.
source: Among protein-level post-translational modifications, phosphorylation is fast and reversible and plays key roles during early embryogenesis: from regulating elements in the Toll and Dpp pathways, to the activation of the Rho Pathway within the mesoderm (Moussian and Roth, 2005; Martin, 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: Differences between embryonic cell populations along the DV axis have been studied with transcriptomic and proteomic methods but with limited depth and temporal resolution.
source: Differences between embryonic cell populations along the DV axis have been studied with transcriptomic and proteomic methods (Casal and Leptin, 1996; Biemar et al., 2006; Gong et al., 2004; Stathopoulos et al., 2002) but with limited depth and temporal resolution.
evidence: This is a statement about prior research in the field, supported by the cited references.

claim: Studies looking at changes over time identified proteins that appear during the maternal to zygotic transition and later in embryogenesis but had no spatial or cell type specificity.
source: Studies looking at changes over time identified proteins that appear during the maternal to zygotic transition (Fabre et al., 2016; Gouw et al., 2009) and later in embryogenesis (Sopko et al., 2014; Casas-Vila et al., 2017), but had no spatial or cell type specificity.
evidence: This is a statement about prior research in the field, supported by the cited references.

claim: None of the previous studies addressed the region-specific post-translational regulation of proteins.
source: None of these studies addressed the region-specific post-translational regulation of proteins.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of prior research.

claim: Many proteins with differences in abundance across the populations do not show the same differences in RNA abundance.
source: We find many proteins with differences in abundance across the populations that do not show the same differences in RNA abundance.
evidence: This is based on the comparison of proteomic data with RNA expression data.

claim: Region-specific phosphorylation patterns exist in proteins that are ubiquitously expressed.
source: We also find region-specific phosphorylation patterns in proteins that are ubiquitously expressed.
evidence: This is based on the phosphoproteomic data analysis.

claim: Networks of phosphoproteins enriched in specific populations included proteasome components, RNA stress granules/P-bodies, adherens junctions associated proteins and microtubule components/associated proteins.
source: Networks of phosphoproteins enriched in specific populations included proteasome components, RNA stress granules/P-bodies, adherens junctions associated proteins and microtubule components/associated proteins.
evidence: This is based on the network analysis of the phosphoproteomic data.

claim: The gd9 allele generates the strongest dorsalization without affecting the length of the embryo.
source: To generate dorsalized embryos we used the gd9 allele, reported to generate the strongest dorsalization without affecting the length of the embryo (Konrad et al., 1988; Ponomareff et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about this mutant allele, supported by the cited references.

claim: Mothers transheterozygous for Tlrm9 and Tlrm10 produce lateralized embryos in which the entire dorso-ventral axis forms neuroectoderm.
source: Mothers transheterozygous for the hypomorphic mutations in Tlrm9 and Tlrm10 were used to produce lateralized embryos, in which the entire dorso-ventral axis forms neuroectoderm (Stathopoulos et al., 2002; Anderson et al., 1985; Cowden and Levine, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge about these mutants, supported by the cited references.

claim: Lateralized and dorsalized embryos from Tlrm10/Tlrm9 and gd9/gd9 mothers expressed neither twist nor snail.
source: 'Lateralized' and 'dorsalized' embryos from Tlrm10/Tlrm9 and gd9/gd9 mothers expressed neither twist nor snail, whereas ventralized embryos from Toll10B/def and spn27Aex/def mothers expressed twist and snail around their entire circumference in the trunk region (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Ventralized embryos from Toll10B/def and spn27Aex/def mothers expressed twist and snail around their entire circumference in the trunk region.
source: 'Lateralized' and 'dorsalized' embryos from Tlrm10/Tlrm9 and gd9/gd9 mothers expressed neither twist nor snail, whereas ventralized embryos from Toll10B/def and spn27Aex/def mothers expressed twist and snail around their entire circumference in the trunk region (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In embryos from Tlrm10/Tlrm9 mothers, sog expression expanded dorsally and ventrally.
source: In embryos from Tlrm10/Tlrm9 mothers, sog expression expanded dorsally and ventrally, whereas dpp expression expanded ventrally (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In embryos from Tlrm10/Tlrm9 mothers, dpp expression expanded ventrally.
source: In embryos from Tlrm10/Tlrm9 mothers, sog expression expanded dorsally and ventrally, whereas dpp expression expanded ventrally (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Ventralized embryos often had a gap in snail expression in a small dorsal-anterior domain around the procephalic furrow.
source: These expression patterns showed some variation and were not entirely homogeneous: ventralized embryos often had a gap in snail expression in a small dorsal-anterior domain around the procephalic furrow.
evidence: This is an observation from the in situ hybridization data.

claim: Ventralized embryos retain some cells with a neuroectodermal fate in a restricted area of the embryo.
source: In this region, we detected sog expression instead, suggesting ventralized embryos retain some cells with a neuroectodermal fate in a restricted area of the embryo (Figure 1B, sog probe).
evidence: This is an inference based on the detection of sog expression in ventralized embryos.

claim: Before gastrulation, all cells have two subpopulations of MTs: a disordered apical network of non-centrosomal MTs with short, non-aligned filaments, and an 'inverted basket' of basal-lateral MTs originating from the centrosomes and enclosing the nucleus.
source: Before gastrulation, all cells have two subpopulations of MTs, which differ in their post-translational modifications: a disordered apical network of non-centrosomal MTs with short, non-aligned filaments, and an 'inverted basket' of basal-lateral MTs originating from the centrosomes and enclosing the nucleus (Takeda et al., 2018; Viswanathan et al., 2019; Figure 7A).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references and confirmed by imaging data in Figure 7A.

claim: The apical population of MTs contains only dynamic MTs, marked by tyrosinated α-tubulin.
source: The apical population contains only dynamic MTs, marked by tyrosinated α-tubulin, whereas the inverted basket also contains stable MTs, marked acetylated α-tubulin (Takeda et al., 2018; Wloga et al., 2017; Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references and confirmed by imaging data.

claim: The inverted basket contains stable MTs, marked by acetylated α-tubulin.
source: The apical population contains only dynamic MTs, marked by tyrosinated α-tubulin, whereas the inverted basket also contains stable MTs, marked acetylated α-tubulin (Takeda et al., 2018; Wloga et al., 2017; Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references and confirmed by imaging data.

claim: During gastrulation MT acetylation patterns change.
source: During gastrulation MT acetylation patterns change.
evidence: This is based on the imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In the ectoderm, MTs become increasingly acetylated but retain their original organization.
source: In the ectoderm, MTs become increasingly acetylated but retain their original organization whereas in central mesodermal cells, the basal-lateral MTs become less acetylated (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on the imaging data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In central mesodermal cells, the basal-lateral MTs become less acetylated during gastrulation.
source: In the ectoderm, MTs become increasingly acetylated but retain their original organization whereas in central mesodermal cells, the basal-lateral MTs become less acetylated (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on the imaging data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Less than 1 min after colcemid injection, most apical filamentous structures, astral MTs emanating from the centrosome, and the centrosomes themselves disappeared.
source: Less than 1 min after the injection, most apical filamentous structures, astral MTs emanating from the centrosome, and the centrosomes themselves disappeared while the stable MTs associated with the nuclear envelope were partially retained (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is based on live imaging data after colcemid injection shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Stable MTs associated with the nuclear envelope were partially retained after colcemid injection.
source: Less than 1 min after the injection, most apical filamentous structures, astral MTs emanating from the centrosome, and the centrosomes themselves disappeared while the stable MTs associated with the nuclear envelope were partially retained (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is based on live imaging data after colcemid injection shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Nuclei normally move basally for 1~2 μm in the last ~20 min of cellularization.
source: Nuclei normally move basally for 1~2 μm in the last ~20 min of cellularization, and this failed in Colcemid-treated embryos, where the nuclei moved slightly further towards the apical cell surface (Figure 7C–K, Videos 1–3).
evidence: This is based on live imaging data shown in Figure 7C-K and Videos 1-3.

claim: In Colcemid-treated embryos, nuclei moved slightly further towards the apical cell surface during cellularization.
source: Nuclei normally move basally for 1~2 μm in the last ~20 min of cellularization, and this failed in Colcemid-treated embryos, where the nuclei moved slightly further towards the apical cell surface (Figure 7C–K, Videos 1–3).
evidence: This is based on live imaging data shown in Figure 7C-K and Videos 1-3.

claim: In normal embryos, nuclei in the constricting ventral furrow cells move a long way from the apical cell surface.
source: In normal embryos, nuclei in the constricting ventral furrow cells move a long way from the apical cell surface.
evidence: This is based on live imaging observations.

claim: In Colcemid-injected embryos, nuclear positioning in ventral furrow cells was more random.
source: In Colcemid-injected embryos, nuclear positioning was more random (Figure 7C and t0; 7L,7M).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of nuclear positions shown in Figure 7L and 7M.

claim: The ventral furrow failed to form in Colcemid-injected embryos.
source: Ultimately, the ventral furrow failed to form (Figure 7C, t0 +10', Video 1).
evidence: This is based on live imaging data shown in Figure 7C and Video 1.

claim: The formation of the cephalic furrow was delayed by 5 min in Colcemid-injected embryos.
source: The formation of the cephalic furrow was delayed by 5 min, but its progress was not affected by Colcemid-treatment (Figure 7F–H, Video 2).
evidence: This is based on live imaging data shown in Figure 7F-H and Video 2.

claim: The progress of cephalic furrow formation was not affected by Colcemid-treatment.
source: The formation of the cephalic furrow was delayed by 5 min, but its progress was not affected by Colcemid-treatment (Figure 7F–H, Video 2).
evidence: This is based on live imaging data shown in Figure 7F-H and Video 2.

claim: Cells on the dorsal ectoderm form an apical dome with a characteristic, curved cell apex.
source: Cells on the dorsal ectoderm form an apical dome with a characteristic, curved cell apex (Figure 7I, t0-5', insets) which is abolished in Colcemid-injected embryos, supporting the model that MT-dependent force is required for apical dome formation (Figure 7I, t0-5', insets).
evidence: This is based on live imaging data shown in Figure 7I.

claim: The apical dome is abolished in Colcemid-injected embryos.
source: Cells on the dorsal ectoderm form an apical dome with a characteristic, curved cell apex (Figure 7I, t0-5', insets) which is abolished in Colcemid-injected embryos, supporting the model that MT-dependent force is required for apical dome formation (Figure 7I, t0-5', insets).
evidence: This is based on live imaging data shown in Figure 7I.

claim: MT-dependent force is required for apical dome formation.
source: Cells on the dorsal ectoderm form an apical dome with a characteristic, curved cell apex (Figure 7I, t0-5', insets) which is abolished in Colcemid-injected embryos, supporting the model that MT-dependent force is required for apical dome formation (Figure 7I, t0-5', insets).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that colcemid treatment abolishes the apical dome.

claim: The dorsal epithelium forms folds which depend on the remodeling of apical MTs, but not on myosin contractility.
source: The dorsal epithelium forms folds which depend on the remodeling of apical MTs, but not on myosin contractility (Rauzi et al., 2015; Takeda et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2012) and involves the descent of the apical dome in initiating cells (Figure 7I, t0 +5').
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: Dome descent does not occur in Colcemid-injected embryos.
source: Dome descent does not occur in Colcemid-injected embryos, and dorsal fold formation eventually fails (Figure 7I, t0 +5', Video 3), supporting the current model that microtubule forces also engage on cell shortening during Dorsal Fold Formation (Takeda et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on live imaging data shown in Figure 7I and Video 3.

claim: Dorsal fold formation eventually fails in Colcemid-injected embryos.
source: Dome descent does not occur in Colcemid-injected embryos, and dorsal fold formation eventually fails (Figure 7I, t0 +5', Video 3), supporting the current model that microtubule forces also engage on cell shortening during Dorsal Fold Formation (Takeda et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on live imaging data shown in Figure 7I and Video 3.

claim: Microtubule forces engage on cell shortening during Dorsal Fold Formation.
source: Dome descent does not occur in Colcemid-injected embryos, and dorsal fold formation eventually fails (Figure 7I, t0 +5', Video 3), supporting the current model that microtubule forces also engage on cell shortening during Dorsal Fold Formation (Takeda et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the colcemid perturbation experiments, supported by cited references.

claim: Blebs in the apical membrane of constricting mesodermal cells were strikingly enlarged after Colcemid injection.
source: Blebs in the apical membrane of constricting mesodermal cells (Costa et al., 1994) were strikingly enlarged after Colcemid injection (Figure 7N).
evidence: This is based on live imaging data shown in Figure 7N.

claim: After Colcemid injection, lateral and dorsal cells accumulate excessive, tortuous subapical membrane.
source: Nevertheless, after Colcemid injection, they accumulate excessive, tortuous subapical membrane (Figure 7O; Figard et al., 2013; Fabrowski et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on live imaging data shown in Figure 7O.

claim: A distinct class of micron-scale membrane blebs form in all dorsal cells during mid to late cellularization.
source: We also observed a distinct class of micron-scale membrane blebs in all dorsal cells, not limited to the dorsal fold initiating cells and unrelated to myosin-dependent apical constriction (Figure 7O). These blebs form during mid to late cellularization, exclude MTs and are stable for minutes.
evidence: This is based on live imaging observations shown in Figure 7O.

claim: The membrane blebs in dorsal cells exclude MTs and are stable for minutes.
source: We also observed a distinct class of micron-scale membrane blebs in all dorsal cells, not limited to the dorsal fold initiating cells and unrelated to myosin-dependent apical constriction (Figure 7O). These blebs form during mid to late cellularization, exclude MTs and are stable for minutes.
evidence: This is based on live imaging observations shown in Figure 7O.

claim: MTs are required for correct nuclear positioning and cell shape homeostasis.
source: In sum, and consistent with a role for microtubules predicted by diffused network analyses, MTs are required for correct nuclear positioning and cell shape homeostasis, and have distinct functional requirements in all three types of epithelial folds during Drosophila gastrulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the colcemid perturbation experiments.

claim: MTs have distinct functional requirements in all three types of epithelial folds during Drosophila gastrulation.
source: In sum, and consistent with a role for microtubules predicted by diffused network analyses, MTs are required for correct nuclear positioning and cell shape homeostasis, and have distinct functional requirements in all three types of epithelial folds during Drosophila gastrulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of colcemid on different regions of the embryo.

claim: Distinct phenotypes of the apical membrane following Colcemid injection suggest differential functionality in the maintenance of membrane-cortex attachment or the dynamics of apical membrane retrieval for MT networks residing on different sides of the embryo.
source: Distinct phenotypes of the apical membrane following Colcemid injection suggest differential functionality in the maintenance of membrane-cortex attachment or the dynamics of apical membrane retrieval for MT networks residing on different sides of the embryo.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed phenotypes after colcemid treatment.

claim: A previous study using 2D gel electrophoresis combined with mass spectrometry identified 37 unique proteins in regional differences of the Drosophila embryo proteome.
source: We can compare our results to a previous study (Gong et al., 2004) on regional differences in the proteome at this stage that used mutants, as we did, to represent different regions of the embryo, and in that regard should be directly comparable. This study was based on 2D gel electrophoresis combined with mass spectrometry, which, while ground-breaking at the time, allowed only a small number (37) of unique proteins to be identified.
evidence: This is a statement about prior research, supported by the cited reference.

claim: All 37 proteins identified in the previous 2D gel study were also detected in the current proteomes.
source: All of these were also detected in our proteomes.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current study's data and a previous study.

claim: Of the proteins with variable isoforms in the previous study, 15 were phosphorylated in the current study.
source: Of the proteins with variable isoforms, we found that 15 were phosphorylated in our own study, of which seven show differences in the mutants, and all of these are consistent with the changes seen in the 2D-PAGE experiment (Gong et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a comparison between the current study's data and a previous study.

claim: Seven of the 15 phosphorylated proteins show differences in the mutants, consistent with the changes seen in the 2D-PAGE experiment.
source: Of the proteins with variable isoforms, we found that 15 were phosphorylated in our own study, of which seven show differences in the mutants, and all of these are consistent with the changes seen in the 2D-PAGE experiment (Gong et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a comparison between the current study's data and a previous study.

claim: Known phosphosites in proteins that act on the Rho-pathway include Sqh-T21, Sqh-S22 and Cofilin-S3.
source: We also detected known phosphosites in proteins that act on the Rho-pathway, such as Sqh-T21, Sqh-S22 and Cofilin-S3 and differentially regulated phosphosites in proteins with key functions at the gastrulation stage, such as LIMK1 and RhoGEF2, and in setting up the DV axis, namely Toll and Cactus.
evidence: This is based on the phosphoproteomic data and established knowledge about these phosphosites.

claim: Differentially regulated phosphosites were detected in proteins with key functions at the gastrulation stage, such as LIMK1 and RhoGEF2.
source: We also detected known phosphosites in proteins that act on the Rho-pathway, such as Sqh-T21, Sqh-S22 and Cofilin-S3 and differentially regulated phosphosites in proteins with key functions at the gastrulation stage, such as LIMK1 and RhoGEF2, and in setting up the DV axis, namely Toll and Cactus.
evidence: This is based on the phosphoproteomic data.

claim: Differentially regulated phosphosites were detected in Toll and Cactus, which are involved in setting up the DV axis.
source: We also detected known phosphosites in proteins that act on the Rho-pathway, such as Sqh-T21, Sqh-S22 and Cofilin-S3 and differentially regulated phosphosites in proteins with key functions at the gastrulation stage, such as LIMK1 and RhoGEF2, and in setting up the DV axis, namely Toll and Cactus.
evidence: This is based on the phosphoproteomic data.

claim: Toll is a known target of the Ser/Thr kinase Pelle.
source: Toll, a known target of the Ser/Thr kinase Pelle (Shen and Manley, 1998), was phosphorylated on serine-871, and this phosphosite was more abundant in ventralized embryos (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: Toll was phosphorylated on serine-871, and this phosphosite was more abundant in ventralized embryos.
source: Toll, a known target of the Ser/Thr kinase Pelle (Shen and Manley, 1998), was phosphorylated on serine-871, and this phosphosite was more abundant in ventralized embryos (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on the phosphoproteomic data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Serines 463, 467, and 468 in Cactus have been shown to be phosphorylated by CKII.
source: This included the serine 871 phosphosite in Toll (Zhai et al., 2008), and serines 463, 467, and 468 in Cactus that have been shown to be phosphorylated by CKII (Liu et al., 1997; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: An Affymetrix-based study using mutants to represent regions along the DV axis identified 23 genes for which the RNA levels were higher in ventralized than in lateralized or dorsalized embryos.
source: For example, an Affymetrix-based study that again used mutants to represent regions along the DV axis of the embryo (Stathopoulos et al., 2002) identified 23 genes for which the RNA levels were higher in ventralized than in lateralized or dorsalized embryos.
evidence: This is a statement about prior research, supported by the cited reference.

claim: Comparing the Affymetrix study to single-cell RNA sequencing data reveals that five genes appear to have little or no dorso-ventral modulation.
source: Comparing those to the expression patterns determined by single-cell RNA sequencing (Karaiskos et al., 2017) reveals that five appear to have little or no dorso-ventral modulation, a result that is also confirmed in the BDGP in situ hybridisation database.
evidence: This is a comparison between different RNA expression datasets.

claim: Genes previously identified by genetic or functional studies and known to be involved in mesoderm development show up in all RNA expression studies.
source: Those genes previously identified by genetic or functional studies, and known to be involved in mesoderm development (including marker genes like twist, snail, zfh1, htl etc) show up in all studies.
evidence: This is a comparison across multiple studies.

claim: The study detected the proteins for 13 of the 17 genes that are seen as ventrally upregulated genes in both the Affymetrix and single-cell RNA sequencing studies.
source: We detect the proteins for 13 of the 17 genes that are seen as ventrally upregulated genes in both studies (Stathopoulos et al., 2002; Karaiskos et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison between the current proteomic data and previous RNA expression studies.

claim: Of the 13 detected proteins, all but four are seen as ventrally upregulated, including known ventral marker genes.
source: Of those, we see all but four as ventrally upregulated, again including known ventral marker genes.
evidence: This is based on the proteomic data analysis.

claim: Traf4 is active in the mesoderm but expressed there at low levels, and becomes expressed in the ectoderm as gastrulation begins.
source: One example is Traf4 (Mathew et al., 2011), which is active in the mesoderm, but expressed there at low levels, and becomes expressed in the ectoderm as gastrulation begins.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: Traf4 was strongly downregulated in the dorsalized embryo but showed only sub-threshold upregulation in the ventralized embryos.
source: In our experiment, it was strongly downregulated in the dorsalized embryo, but showed only sub-threshold upregulation in the ventralized embryos.
evidence: This is based on the proteomic data.

claim: The network analysis identified the cullin complex as differentially expressed and differentially regulated.
source: The network analysis identified the cullin complex as differentially expressed and differentially regulated (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on the network analysis of the proteomic data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Neur is found in increased abundance ventrally.
source: We also find Neur in increased abundance ventrally.
evidence: This is based on the proteomic data.

claim: An enrichment of P-granule-related networks was found both in the proteome and the phosphoproteome.
source: Another mechanism for post-transcriptional gene regulation is the differential translation or degradation of mRNAs along the dorso-ventral axis, and we find an enrichment of P-granule-related networks both in the proteome and the phosphoproteome.
evidence: This is based on the network analysis of the proteomic and phosphoproteomic data.

claim: P-granule-related networks are enriched within DV clusters with complete or partial ectodermal fate.
source: These networks are enriched within DV clusters with complete or partial ectodermal fate, that is the same clusters that show a strong uncoupling between mRNA and protein abundance (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on the network analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Nearly all studied genes in larval tissues derived from the ectoderm and neuroectoderm show mRNA/protein discordance.
source: Partial agreement between mRNA and protein spatial distribution is not an exclusive feature of the gastrula: it has also been described for larval tissues derived from the ectoderm and neuroectoderm, where nearly all studied genes show mRNA/protein discordance (Titlow et al., 2023; 97.5%; N=200 proteins).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: The uncoupling between mRNA and protein abundance seems to be the rule rather than exception in ectodermal and neuroectodermal tissues.
source: Therefore, the uncoupling between mRNA and protein abundance seems to be the rule rather than exception in at least these tissues, highlighting the importance of post-transcriptional regulation on gene expression regulation during development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited reference and the current study's findings.

claim: Microtubules are often required for cell shape homeostasis in epithelial tissues.
source: The diffused networks also showed phosphorylation of microtubules as a differentiating mechanism along the dorso-ventral axis during gastrulation, an interesting finding, because in epithelial tissues microtubules are often required for cell shape homeostasis (Picone et al., 2010; Gomez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: Morphogenetic cell shape changes in Drosophila for which microtubules are essential include the squamous morphogenesis of the amnioserosa.
source: Morphogenetic cell shape changes in Drosophila for which microtubules are essential include the squamous morphogenesis of the amnioserosa (Pope and Harris, 2008) and the invagination of the mesoderm (Ko et al., 2019) and the salivary placode (Booth et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: Dorsal fold formation requires microtubules.
source: Here, we found that dorsal fold formation also requires microtubules.
evidence: This is based on the colcemid perturbation experiments.

claim: Ventral furrow and dorsal fold formation differ in their dependency on myosin.
source: Ventral furrow and dorsal fold formation differ in their dependency on myosin (Rauzi et al., 2015; Martin, 2020), but our results show that both require microtubules for the basal relocalisation of nuclei.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references, combined with the current study's findings.

claim: Both ventral furrow and dorsal fold formation require microtubules for the basal relocalisation of nuclei.
source: Ventral furrow and dorsal fold formation differ in their dependency on myosin (Rauzi et al., 2015; Martin, 2020), but our results show that both require microtubules for the basal relocalisation of nuclei.
evidence: This is based on the colcemid perturbation experiments.

claim: The requirement for microtubules in nuclear repositioning is functionally distinct from the association of microtubules with actomyosin during myosin-dependent tissue folding.
source: This requirement is functionally distinct from the association of microtubules with actomyosin during myosin-dependent tissue folding (Ko et al., 2019; Booth et al., 2014; Manning et al., 2013) and instead, may relate to the classic role of microtubules in vectorial trafficking and organelle localisation (de Forges et al., 2012; Burute and Kapitein, 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results and established knowledge about microtubule functions.

claim: One reason why nuclei need to be actively repositioned may be that in their apical location they constitute a physical barrier to the cell's apical constriction.
source: One reason why nuclei need to be actively repositioned may be that in their apical location they constitute a physical barrier to the cell's apical constriction.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed requirement for nuclear repositioning.

claim: Both Toll10B and spn27A ventralising mutations produced embryos that recapitulated known biological qualities of the mesoderm along the entire DV axis.
source: Both Toll10B and spn27A ventralising mutations produced embryos that recapitulated known biological qualities of the mesoderm along the entire DV axis, such as the expression of ventral fate determinants, or the apical localisation of the adherens junctions.
evidence: This is based on the immunostaining and in situ hybridization data.

claim: The similarities between Toll10B and spn27A embryos were not fully mirrored in their proteomes.
source: However, these similarities were not fully mirrored in their proteomes.
evidence: This is based on the proteomic data analysis.

claim: The spn27A proteome seemed to be more similar to the dorsalized than to the Toll10B proteome.
source: Curiously, the spn27A proteome seemed to be more similar to the dorsalized than to the Toll10B proteome which would indicate that Toll10B embryos are 'more' ventral than spn27A embryos.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation analysis of the proteomes.

claim: Most of the mesodermal marker genes are more abundant in spn27A embryos than in Toll10B embryos.
source: However, most of the mesodermal marker genes (snail, twist, mdr49, wntD, neur) make an exception are more abundant in spn27A embryos.
evidence: This is based on the proteomic data.

claim: Ectodermal fate markers are more strongly downregulated in spn27A than in Toll10B embryos.
source: Similarly ectodermal fate markers are more strongly downregulated in spn27A than in Toll10B embryos.
evidence: This is based on the proteomic data.

claim: Toll10B mutants fail to repress the expression of ectodermal genes such as egr, zen and crb.
source: Specifically, Toll10B mutants fail to repress the expression of ectodermal genes such as egr, zen and crb.
evidence: This is based on the proteomic data.

claim: Spn27A is a serine protease inhibitor of the pathway that creates the active form of Spätzle.
source: Spn27A is a serine protease inhibitor of the pathway that creates the active form of Spätzle (Spz), the ligand for Toll.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Toll signaling pathway.

claim: Both Toll10B and spn27A mutations lead to constitutive activity of Toll.
source: Both mutations lead to constitutive activity of Toll, Toll10B through a mutation in the receptor itself (Schneider et al., 1991; Erdélyi and Szabad, 1989), spn27A through enabling a homogeneously high level of Spz along the DV axis (rather than a peak on the ventral side; Ligoxygakis et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge about these mutations, supported by the cited references.

claim: Toll10B leads to constitutive activity through a mutation in the receptor itself.
source: Both mutations lead to constitutive activity of Toll, Toll10B through a mutation in the receptor itself (Schneider et al., 1991; Erdélyi and Szabad, 1989), spn27A through enabling a homogeneously high level of Spz along the DV axis (rather than a peak on the ventral side; Ligoxygakis et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: spn27A leads to constitutive Toll activity through enabling a homogeneously high level of Spz along the DV axis.
source: Both mutations lead to constitutive activity of Toll, Toll10B through a mutation in the receptor itself (Schneider et al., 1991; Erdélyi and Szabad, 1989), spn27A through enabling a homogeneously high level of Spz along the DV axis (rather than a peak on the ventral side; Ligoxygakis et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: Spz is highly abundant and should not be a limiting factor for the activation of Toll.
source: Because Spz is highly abundant it should not be a limiting factor for the activation of Toll (Morisalo and Anderson, 1995; Schneider et al., 1994; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and loss of Spn27A should enable the full activation of Toll along the embryonic DV axis.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references and the proteomic data.

claim: Loss of Spn27A should enable the full activation of Toll along the embryonic DV axis.
source: Because Spz is highly abundant it should not be a limiting factor for the activation of Toll (Morisalo and Anderson, 1995; Schneider et al., 1994; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and loss of Spn27A should enable the full activation of Toll along the embryonic DV axis.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge and the proteomic data.

claim: Constitutively active Toll does not lead to the same level of signaling as the binding of the ligand to the receptor.
source: Our results indicate that constitutively active Toll does not lead to the same level of signaling as the binding of the ligand to the receptor, and that these different levels lead to unexpected differences in the downstream targets of the signaling pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteomic differences between Toll10B and spn27A embryos.

claim: Different levels of Toll signaling lead to unexpected differences in the downstream targets of the signaling pathway.
source: Our results indicate that constitutively active Toll does not lead to the same level of signaling as the binding of the ligand to the receptor, and that these different levels lead to unexpected differences in the downstream targets of the signaling pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteomic differences between Toll10B and spn27A embryos.

claim: The 'linear model' is based on the assumption that each mutant embryo faithfully represents one defined area of cells along the DV axis of the embryo.
source: The 'linear model' we formulated is based on the assumption that each mutant embryo faithfully represents one defined area of cells along the DV axis of the embryo, and that the full set of cell types in the embryo can therefore be reconstituted as the sum of the mutant cell types – weighted according to the area they occupy in the embryo.
evidence: This is an explanation of the analytical approach developed in the study.

claim: The linear model was found to be true not only for proteins that occur at equal level in all genotypes, but also for most of the differentially modulated proteins.
source: We found this to be true not only for the trivial cases of those proteins that occur at equal level in all genotypes, but also for most of the differentially modulated proteins.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of the proteomic data using the linear model.

claim: Strong deviations from the linear model may indicate non-autonomous regulation.
source: Thus, wherever an interaction between the cell populations in the embryo is necessary for generating the correct expression or phosphorylation level, the linear model we proposed no longer applies; this means that strong deviations may indicate non-autonomous regulation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the deviations from the linear model.

claim: Ind is an outlier with higher than predicted expression in the dorsalized and ventralized mutants, consistent with repressive input from these regions in the wildtype.
source: We indeed find that one of those proteins, Ind, is an outlier (deviation = 2.6) with higher than predicted expression in the dorsalized and ventralized mutants, consistent with repressive input from these regions in the wildtype.
evidence: This is based on the deviation analysis and established knowledge about Ind regulation.

claim: TM9SF4 is present in all mutants at nearly 100-fold higher levels than in the wildtype.
source: This is illustrated by the most extreme example, TM9SF4, which encodes an immune-related transporter that is present in all mutants at nearly 100-fold higher levels than in the wildtype.
evidence: This is based on the proteomic data.

claim: Stress-related categories represented only a small percentage of proteins and phosphoproteins with the highest deviations.
source: However, we did not find that this was a general rule either in the proteomes or in the phosphoproteomes: stress-related categories such as those from the 'chaperone' or 'immune response' ontology classes represented only a small percentage of proteins and phosphoproteins with the highest deviations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: This is based on the ontology analysis of proteins with extreme deviations.

claim: 5883 proteins were detected in wild type embryos.
source: A total of 5883 of these were detected in wild type embryos (Figure 2A), exceeding previously reported number identified by proteomic approaches in early Drosophila embryogenesis (Casas-Vila et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The number of proteins detected in wild type embryos exceeds previously reported numbers identified by proteomic approaches in early Drosophila embryogenesis.
source: A total of 5883 of these were detected in wild type embryos (Figure 2A), exceeding previously reported number identified by proteomic approaches in early Drosophila embryogenesis (Casas-Vila et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison between the current study's data and a previous study.

claim: Most proteins were detected in all genotypes.
source: Most were detected in all genotypes (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on the intersection analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 519 proteins had restricted detection including the DV fate determinants Doc1, Snail, Twist, and dMyc.
source: The small number (519/6111) with restricted detection included the DV fate determinants Doc1, Snail, Twist, and dMyc (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is based on the proteomic data and shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Only 73% of phosphosites were found across all genotypes.
source: Only 73% of phosphosites were found across all genotypes (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on the intersection analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Twenty-eight percent of the proteins differed significantly in an ANOVA test across all five populations.
source: Twenty-eight percent of the proteins (1699/6111) and 9% of the phosphosites (573/6259) differed significantly in an ANOVA test across all five populations (wild type and four mutants; permutation-based FDR <0.1, s0=0.1).
evidence: This is based on the statistical analysis of the proteomic data.

claim: Nine percent of the phosphosites differed significantly in an ANOVA test across all five populations.
source: Twenty-eight percent of the proteins (1699/6111) and 9% of the phosphosites (573/6259) differed significantly in an ANOVA test across all five populations (wild type and four mutants; permutation-based FDR <0.1, s0=0.1).
evidence: This is based on the statistical analysis of the phosphoproteomic data.

claim: The enrichment for proteins or phosphosites in the mutant genotypes over the wild-type ranged from near-zero to 100 fold.
source: The enrichment for proteins or phosphosites in the mutant genotypes over the wild-type ranged from near-zero to 100 fold (Figure 2G and H) with about half changing by less than 1.5-fold.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of fold changes shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: About half of the proteins and phosphosites changed by less than 1.5-fold.
source: The enrichment for proteins or phosphosites in the mutant genotypes over the wild-type ranged from near-zero to 100 fold (Figure 2G and H) with about half changing by less than 1.5-fold.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of fold changes shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: The fold-changes for Snail measured in spn27Aex/def was 7.7 fold.
source: The fold-changes for the mesodermal fate determinants Snail (7.7 fold) and Twist (14.6 fold) measured in spn27Aex/def were the largest positive fold-changes among the DV fate determinants (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is based on the proteomic data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The fold-changes for Twist measured in spn27Aex/def was 14.6 fold.
source: The fold-changes for the mesodermal fate determinants Snail (7.7 fold) and Twist (14.6 fold) measured in spn27Aex/def were the largest positive fold-changes among the DV fate determinants (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is based on the proteomic data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Both Toll and Spn27A were detected and each of them was reduced in abundance in the respective mutant embryos.
source: We detected both Toll and Spn27A, and each of them was reduced in abundance in the respective mutant embryos. (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on the proteomic data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Snail, Twist, Mdr49, Traf4, and CG4500 were more abundant in ventralized embryos.
source: Proteins that are known to be expressed differentially along the DV axis (Figure 1A) were more abundant in the appropriate genotypes: Snail, Twist, Mdr49, Traf4, and CG4500 in ventralized embryos; the pro-neuroectodermal (lateral) factor Sog in lateralized embryos; pro-ectodermal (dorsal) factors Zen, Doc1, Dtg, Net, and Egr in dorsalized embryos (Figure 1D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D; p values for all comparisons in all figures are summarized in Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on the proteomic data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: The pro-neuroectodermal factor Sog was more abundant in lateralized embryos.
source: Proteins that are known to be expressed differentially along the DV axis (Figure 1A) were more abundant in the appropriate genotypes: Snail, Twist, Mdr49, Traf4, and CG4500 in ventralized embryos; the pro-neuroectodermal (lateral) factor Sog in lateralized embryos; pro-ectodermal (dorsal) factors Zen, Doc1, Dtg, Net, and Egr in dorsalized embryos (Figure 1D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D; p values for all comparisons in all figures are summarized in Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on the proteomic data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Pro-ectodermal factors Zen, Doc1, Dtg, Net, and Egr were more abundant in dorsalized embryos.
source: Proteins that are known to be expressed differentially along the DV axis (Figure 1A) were more abundant in the appropriate genotypes: Snail, Twist, Mdr49, Traf4, and CG4500 in ventralized embryos; the pro-neuroectodermal (lateral) factor Sog in lateralized embryos; pro-ectodermal (dorsal) factors Zen, Doc1, Dtg, Net, and Egr in dorsalized embryos (Figure 1D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D; p values for all comparisons in all figures are summarized in Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on the proteomic data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Known ventral-specific proteins were more strongly upregulated in serpin27A embryos than in Toll10B.
source: Known ventral-specific proteins (Snail, Twist, Mdr49, and CG4500) were more strongly upregulated in serpin27A embryos than in Toll10B, and most dorsal-specific proteins (e.g. Egr, Zen, Sdt, Net, and Ptr) were more strongly downregulated.
evidence: This is based on the proteomic data.

claim: Most dorsal-specific proteins were more strongly downregulated in serpin27A embryos than in Toll10B.
source: Known ventral-specific proteins (Snail, Twist, Mdr49, and CG4500) were more strongly upregulated in serpin27A embryos than in Toll10B, and most dorsal-specific proteins (e.g. Egr, Zen, Sdt, Net, and Ptr) were more strongly downregulated.
evidence: This is based on the proteomic data.

claim: 1765 of the phospho-proteins (96%) were ones that were also found in the proteome.
source: 1765 of the phospho-proteins (96%) we identified were ones that we also found in the proteome, whereas 82 had not been detected in the proteome (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on the comparison between proteomic and phosphoproteomic data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 82 phospho-proteins had not been detected in the proteome.
source: 1765 of the phospho-proteins (96%) we identified were ones that we also found in the proteome, whereas 82 had not been detected in the proteome (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on the comparison between proteomic and phosphoproteomic data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Most of the changes in phosphorylation were in proteins for which the level of the host protein was unchanged.
source: We found that most of the changes in phosphorylation were in proteins for which the level of the host protein was unchanged (black and white boxes in Figure 5B; 67 to 82% of the protein-phosphosite pairs).
evidence: This is based on the correlation analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: 67 to 82% of the protein-phosphosite pairs showed changes in phosphorylation without changes in host protein levels.
source: We found that most of the changes in phosphorylation were in proteins for which the level of the host protein was unchanged (black and white boxes in Figure 5B; 67 to 82% of the protein-phosphosite pairs).
evidence: This is based on the correlation analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Among phosphosites for which the host protein showed differential abundance, 7–13% changed in the same direction.
source: Among those for which the host protein showed differential abundance, 7–13% of their phosphosites changed in the same direction (both protein abundance and phosphorylation up, or both down), and 10–19% changed in the opposite direction.
evidence: This is based on the correlation analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Among phosphosites for which the host protein showed differential abundance, 10–19% changed in the opposite direction.
source: Among those for which the host protein showed differential abundance, 7–13% of their phosphosites changed in the same direction (both protein abundance and phosphorylation up, or both down), and 10–19% changed in the opposite direction.
evidence: This is based on the correlation analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The majority of the phosphosites fitted the 'linear model'.
source: We tested if the phospho-proteomes fitted the 'linear model' (i.e. whether the sum of the weighted mutant values corresponded to the measured values in the wildtype) and found that the majority of the phosphosites did (Figure 5C, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is based on the deviation analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Among the strongly deviating phosphoproteins, there are a number of kinases with known morphogenetic functions, such as Par-1, SRC42A and nucleoside-diphosphate kinase (awd).
source: Among the strongly deviating phosphoproteins, we find a number of kinases with known morphogenetic functions, such as Par-1, SRC42A and nucleoside-diphosphate kinase (awd) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, Supplementary file 13).
evidence: This is based on the deviation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The two ventralising mutants clustered together in the phosphoproteome analysis.
source: The two ventralising mutants now clustered together, and the dorsalized mutant showed the most distinct behavior (Figure 5G, compare to Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on the correlation analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The dorsalized mutant showed the most distinct behavior in the phosphoproteome analysis.
source: The two ventralising mutants now clustered together, and the dorsalized mutant showed the most distinct behavior (Figure 5G, compare to Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on the correlation analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Of 24 proteins associated with Rho signaling, 21 were detected in the wild type and at least one of the mutants.
source: Of 24 proteins associated with Rho signaling, we detected 21 in the wild type and at least one of the mutants (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on the proteomic data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Most Rho pathway proteins occurred at similar levels in all genotypes, except Cofilin/Twinstar, Moesin, and Profilin/chickadee, which were more abundant in the ectodermal cell populations.
source: Most, including the myosin light chain, occurred at similar levels in all genotypes, except Cofilin/Twinstar, Moesin, and Profilin/chickadee, which were more abundant in the ectodermal cell populations (clusters D and DL).
evidence: This is based on the proteomic data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Fourteen of the 21 Rho pathway proteins were phosphorylated.
source: Fourteen of the 21 proteins were phosphorylated.
evidence: This is based on the phosphoproteomic data.

claim: The phosphorylation of the Cofilin/Twinstar kinase LIMK1 and phosphatase Slingshot were modulated in the D and DL clusters.
source: These included the known phosphosites in myosin light chain (MLC) and Cofilin/Twinstar (Figure 5F, no statistical differences across genotypes for Sqh and Cofilin phosphosites, see Supplementary file 2), and the phosphorylation of the Cofilin/Twinstar kinase LIMK1 and phosphatase Slingshot (ssh), which were modulated in the D and DL clusters, as were RhoGEF2 and the MLC phosphatase Mbs (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on the phosphoproteomic data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: RhoGEF2 and the MLC phosphatase Mbs were modulated in the D and DL clusters.
source: These included the known phosphosites in myosin light chain (MLC) and Cofilin/Twinstar (Figure 5F, no statistical differences across genotypes for Sqh and Cofilin phosphosites, see Supplementary file 2), and the phosphorylation of the Cofilin/Twinstar kinase LIMK1 and phosphatase Slingshot (ssh), which were modulated in the D and DL clusters, as were RhoGEF2 and the MLC phosphatase Mbs (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on the phosphoproteomic data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: A diffusion-based algorithm was used on each of the DV clusters to systematically find networks.
source: To systematically find such networks, we used a diffusion-based algorithm (Giudice et al., 2024) on each of the DV clusters.
evidence: This is a description of the analytical method used.

claim: The starting weight of each protein in the network analysis was based on either its euclidean distance score or on the deviation from the linear model.
source: The starting weight of each protein was based on either on its euclidean distance score ('ED', Supplementary file 11) or on the deviation from the linear model ('Dev', Supplementary file 6 and 10).
evidence: This is a description of the analytical method used.

claim: An ego network analysis yielded a set of 83 ontology terms in the proteome and 87 in the phospho-proteome that were significantly enriched in one or more networks.
source: An ego network analysis (see Methods) yielded a set of 83 ontology terms in the proteome and 87 in the phospho-proteome that were significantly enriched in one or more networks.
evidence: This is based on the network analysis of the proteomic and phosphoproteomic data.

claim: Both proteomic and phosphoproteomic experiments were highly enriched for cellular components associated with DNA and RNA metabolism or the regulation of gene expression.
source: The heatmaps illustrate that both experiments were highly enriched for cellular components associated with DNA and RNA metabolism or the regulation of gene expression.
evidence: This is based on the network analysis shown in the heatmaps.

claim: The majority of the enriched proteins and phosphoproteins were characterized as nuclear ontology classes.
source: In agreement with this, the majority of the enriched proteins and phosphoproteins were characterized as nuclear ontology classes.
evidence: This is based on the ontology analysis of the network data.

claim: Networks enriched for cytoskeletal components were much more prevalent in the phosphoproteomes than in the proteomes.
source: In the phosphoproteomes the networks enriched for cytoskeletal components were much more prevalent in the phosphoproteomes (14 of 62) than in the proteomes (3 of 63), with microtubules strongly represented (12 of 14 cellular components), in particular the alpha and beta tubulins and microtubule associated proteins (Supplementary file 12).
evidence: This is based on the network analysis of the proteomic and phosphoproteomic data.

claim: Microtubules were strongly represented in the cytoskeletal networks enriched in the phosphoproteomes.
source: In the phosphoproteomes the networks enriched for cytoskeletal components were much more prevalent in the phosphoproteomes (14 of 62) than in the proteomes (3 of 63), with microtubules strongly represented (12 of 14 cellular components), in particular the alpha and beta tubulins and microtubule associated proteins (Supplementary file 12).
evidence: This is based on the network analysis of the phosphoproteomic data.

claim: The cell cortex is among the enriched components in the network analysis.
source: Cytoskeletal proteins are often localized in the cell cortex, and we indeed find this association reflected in the results of the network analysis. The cell cortex is among the enriched components, and among the proteins in this category, we find cytoskeletal elements.
evidence: This is based on the network analysis.

claim: Networks that include the actin-microtubule crosslinker Shot and the actin polymerase Profilin are enriched in the dorsal cluster.
source: For example, networks that include the actin-microtubule crosslinker Shot and the actin polymerase Profilin are enriched in the dorsal cluster; networks that include the apical polarity determinant Stardust or the Hippo pathway component Warts in the dorso-lateral cluster.
evidence: This is based on the network analysis.

claim: Networks that include the apical polarity determinant Stardust or the Hippo pathway component Warts are enriched in the dorso-lateral cluster.
source: For example, networks that include the actin-microtubule crosslinker Shot and the actin polymerase Profilin are enriched in the dorsal cluster; networks that include the apical polarity determinant Stardust or the Hippo pathway component Warts in the dorso-lateral cluster.
evidence: This is based on the network analysis.

claim: A phosphoprotein network associated with adherens junctions and zonula adherens, containing the junction-actin connectors Canoe and Girdin, was enriched in the D cluster.
source: A phosphoprotein network associated with adherens junctions and zonula adherens, one of which contains the junction-actin connectors Canoe and Girdin (Houssin et al., 2015; Sawyer et al., 2009) was enriched in the D cluster (Supplementary file 12).
evidence: This is based on the network analysis of the phosphoproteomic data.

claim: The adherens junctions relocalize apically in the ventralized mutants.
source: We find that, as in the mesoderm of wildtype embryos, the adherens junctions (as visualized by immunostaining for Armadillo/β-Catenin; Figure 1C) relocalize apically in the ventralized mutants, but remain apico-lateral in lateralized and shift slightly more basally in dorsalized mutants, again mirroring the morphology of lateral and dorsal regions of the wildtype embryo (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The adherens junctions remain apico-lateral in lateralized mutants.
source: We find that, as in the mesoderm of wildtype embryos, the adherens junctions (as visualized by immunostaining for Armadillo/β-Catenin; Figure 1C) relocalize apically in the ventralized mutants, but remain apico-lateral in lateralized and shift slightly more basally in dorsalized mutants, again mirroring the morphology of lateral and dorsal regions of the wildtype embryo (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The adherens junctions shift slightly more basally in dorsalized mutants.
source: We find that, as in the mesoderm of wildtype embryos, the adherens junctions (as visualized by immunostaining for Armadillo/β-Catenin; Figure 1C) relocalize apically in the ventralized mutants, but remain apico-lateral in lateralized and shift slightly more basally in dorsalized mutants, again mirroring the morphology of lateral and dorsal regions of the wildtype embryo (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The apical actomyosin network forms a pulsatile apical network in ventralized embryos.
source: Similarly, the apical actomyosin network, which we characterized in living embryos expressing a fluorescently tagged myosin light chain (sqh-mCherry, Figure 1E and F) forms a pulsatile apical network in ventralized embryos, whereas myosin accumulates at cell junctions in lateralized embryos, and dorsalized embryos dissolve the loose apical actomyosin of the early blastoderm (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is based on live imaging data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Myosin accumulates at cell junctions in lateralized embryos.
source: Similarly, the apical actomyosin network, which we characterized in living embryos expressing a fluorescently tagged myosin light chain (sqh-mCherry, Figure 1E and F) forms a pulsatile apical network in ventralized embryos, whereas myosin accumulates at cell junctions in lateralized embryos, and dorsalized embryos dissolve the loose apical actomyosin of the early blastoderm (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is based on live imaging data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Dorsalized embryos dissolve the loose apical actomyosin of the early blastoderm.
